title: GOD CLOSED THE WOMBS OF AN ENTIRE ROYAL HOUSEHOLD BECAUSE A KING HAD TAKEN ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE.
paragraphs: GOD CLOSED THE WOMBS OF AN ENTIRE ROYAL HOUSEHOLD BECAUSE A KING HAD TAKEN ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE.
But the most shocking part of this biblical scandal is that God confronted a king, protected a woman, corrected a prophet, and demonstrated a mercy that none of them could afford to take for granted.
Imagine going to sleep as a powerful king, believing everything in your kingdom is under control, only to hear God Himself tell you in a dream:
“Behold, thou art but a dead man.”
— Genesis 20:3, KJV
No invading army.
No assassination plot.
No rebellion threatening your throne.
Just God confronting you over a woman you had brought into your household.
And what makes this story even more disturbing is that the king did not initially know the woman was married.
He had been deceived.
The man responsible for that deception was not some godless criminal or notorious enemy of Israel.
It was Abraham.
The father of faith.
The man who had received extraordinary promises from God.
The man whose descendants would eventually become a great nation.
Yes, even a man who walked with God could become so consumed by fear that he compromised the truth and endangered someone he was supposed to protect.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story begins to feel uncomfortably personal.
Because sometimes the greatest scandals do not begin with hatred, lust, or rebellion.
Sometimes they begin with fear.
Fear of losing someone.
Fear of being rejected.
Fear of suffering.
Fear of losing control.
Fear that makes us manipulate circumstances instead of trusting the God we claim to believe in.
Abraham had journeyed into Gerar, where Abimelech ruled as king. Concerned that he might be killed because of Sarah, Abraham introduced her as his sister.
There was an element of truth in his statement. According to Genesis 20:12, Sarah was his half-sister.
But she was also his wife.
And Abraham deliberately concealed the truth that mattered most.
A half-truth becomes deception when it is used to make someone believe a lie.
How many relationships have been destroyed that way?
How many marriages have suffered because someone insisted they technically did not lie?
How many Christians have justified dishonesty because telling the whole truth would cost them something?
We reveal enough information to appear innocent while hiding enough information to escape accountability.
We call it protecting ourselves.
Sometimes, Scripture calls it deception.
Abimelech took Sarah into his household, unaware that she belonged to an existing marriage covenant.
But before he could touch her, God intervened.
Genesis 20:3 records God's warning:
“Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man's wife.”
The original Hebrew describes Sarah as:
בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל — be'ulat ba'al
An expression meaning a married woman, a woman who has a husband.
The issue was not simply that Abimelech had taken a woman whom Abraham loved. Sarah was already bound within a marriage covenant.
God recognized that covenant even when Abraham's deception had concealed it from everyone else.
The king's authority did not give him permission to violate it.
His wealth could not purchase an exemption.
His ignorance did not make the situation something God would simply overlook.
But what happens next reveals something extraordinary about God's justice.
Abimelech responded:
“Lord, wilt thou slay also a righteous nation?”
— Genesis 20:4, KJV
He explained that Abraham had called Sarah his sister and that Sarah had also identified Abraham as her brother.
Then he appealed to the integrity of his heart and the innocence of his hands.
And God acknowledged his integrity.
Genesis 20:6 contains one of the most revealing statements about divine restraint in the entire narrative:
וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ גַּם־אָנֹכִי אוֹתְךָ מֵחֲטוֹ־לִי
Va'echsokh gam-anokhi otekha mechatō-li.
Meaning, “I also restrained you from sinning against Me.”
Read that again.
God did not merely expose a dangerous situation after the damage had been done.
He prevented Abimelech from committing the offense.
There was a sin the king might have committed, a covenant he might have violated, and consequences he might have brought upon himself.
But God restrained him.
Sometimes mercy does not arrive looking like an open door.
Sometimes mercy is the door that refuses to open.
Sometimes it is the opportunity that disappears, the temptation that gets interrupted, or the truth that comes out before the damage becomes irreversible.
Not every disappointment is divine intervention, and Scripture does not authorize us to interpret every closed door as a direct message from heaven.
But Genesis 20 reminds us that God is capable of protecting us even from dangers we do not yet understand.
How many times have we thanked God for the blessings we received but forgotten to thank Him for the sins His grace helped us avoid?
How many things would we have destroyed if every selfish desire had been granted?
How many times have we mistaken unrestricted freedom for blessing when what we desperately needed was restraint?
Abimelech had power.
But power without restraint can become destruction.
And God loved righteousness too much to allow this situation to continue unchallenged.
Then comes the part of the story that many people overlook.
Genesis 20:17–18 says:
“So Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children.
For the LORD had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham's wife.”
The Hebrew wording is particularly emphatic:
כִּי־עָצֹר עָצַר יְהוָה בְּעַד כָּל־רֶחֶם
Ki-atsor atsar YHWH be'ad kol-rechem.
The expression atsor atsar combines the Hebrew infinitive absolute with a finite verb from the same root, intensifying the action.
It communicates that the LORD had indeed, or completely, closed every womb within Abimelech's household.
This was not presented as an ordinary medical occurrence.
Within this particular biblical narrative, Scripture explicitly identifies God's intervention and connects it to the situation involving Sarah.
An entire royal household experienced the consequences of a crisis that began with deception and the taking of another man's wife.
What began as Abraham's attempt to protect himself became a crisis involving people far beyond himself.
Sin rarely respects the boundaries of the person who commits it.
A father's dishonesty can wound his children.
A mother's bitterness can poison relationships.
A husband's unfaithfulness can devastate an entire family.
A leader's secret compromise can shake a whole congregation.
One person's decisions can leave other people carrying pain they never chose.
That does not mean everyone who suffers is personally guilty of the sin that caused their suffering.
And this distinction matters deeply.
If you are struggling with infertility, please do not read Genesis 20 as a declaration that God is punishing you for hidden sin.
Scripture gives us no authority to make that accusation.
Elizabeth and Zechariah were described as righteous before God, yet they experienced childlessness for many years (Luke 1:6–7).
Jesus Himself rejected the simplistic assumption that every physical affliction must be traced to a particular person's sin (John 9:1–3).
Your empty nursery is not evidence that God has rejected you.
Your unanswered prayers are not proof that your faith is defective.
Your tears are not a confession of guilt.
Genesis 20 describes a specific act of divine judgment and intervention. It is not a universal explanation for infertility.
Never weaponize a passage of Scripture against someone whose heart is already breaking.
But there is another uncomfortable truth in this story.
Abimelech, the foreign king, confronted Abraham, the prophet of God, about his dishonesty.
“What hast thou done unto us?”
— Genesis 20:9, KJV
Imagine the humiliation.
The man who knew God's promises was being questioned about his moral conduct by the man he had deceived.
Abraham had assumed that there was no fear of God in Gerar.
Yet Abimelech demonstrated a moral concern that exposed Abraham's own compromise.
The believer had misjudged the outsider.
The prophet had acted out of fear.
The man with the covenant promises had failed to trust the One who made them.
Does that sound familiar?
Sometimes we are so busy identifying the darkness in the world that we refuse to confront the darkness in ourselves.
We condemn unbelievers for dishonesty while making excuses for our own.
We demand repentance from strangers while protecting our favorite sins.
We quote Scripture publicly while privately violating the principles we preach.
We know how to look spiritual.
But looking spiritual and living surrendered are not the same thing.
A Bible verse in your biography cannot substitute for integrity in your relationships.
A ministry title cannot sanctify manipulation.
Years of serving God do not make you incapable of falling into sin.
Abraham's story is not permission to compromise.
It is a warning against spiritual pride.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years pretending that everything is fine.
You know what people would think if they discovered the whole truth.
You know which conversations you have avoided.
You know which apologies you owe.
You know which secrets you have protected.
You know the difference between the person people celebrate and the person you become when nobody is watching.
And you are exhausted.
Exhausted from managing appearances.
Exhausted from defending decisions you know were wrong.
Exhausted from asking God to bless a life you are unwilling to surrender.
You do not have to disclose your private struggles publicly. But you do need to bring them honestly before Christ.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
But as a sincere expression of your desire to stop hiding and begin walking in truth.
Because the most beautiful part of Genesis 20 is not that God closed the wombs.
It is that God restored what had been afflicted.
God instructed Abimelech to return Sarah to Abraham.
Abimelech obeyed.
He returned her, gave gifts, and publicly addressed the situation.
Abraham then prayed for him.
And God healed the household.
The same God who confronted the scandal made restoration possible.
But notice something astonishing.
God still identified Abraham as a prophet in Genesis 20:7, despite Abraham's failure.
That did not mean God approved of his deception.
It meant Abraham's failure had not erased God's covenant purposes.
God's grace is not an endorsement of everything His people do.
It is His undeserved kindness toward people who could never establish their own righteousness before Him.
Abraham was not the hero because he never failed.
God was faithful even when Abraham failed to demonstrate the faithfulness he should have.
And this is where the story begins to point us toward something greater.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, through the very covenant line God had promised to Abraham, the Savior would enter human history.
Matthew 1:1 introduces Jesus as the son of David and the son of Abraham.
The Messiah came through a family history containing deception, brokenness, moral failure, suffering, and scandal.
Yet Jesus Himself was without sin.
Where human beings compromised, Christ remained faithful.
Where we concealed the truth, Christ embodied the truth.
Where we attempted to save ourselves at the expense of others, Jesus willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
Abraham endangered another person because he feared for his own life.
Jesus laid down His own life for the salvation of others.
What a breathtaking contrast.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek word used for sinners is ἁμαρτωλῶν — hamartōlōn, referring to those who are sinful.
Christ did not wait for us to become morally impressive before demonstrating His love.
He came for sinners.
He died for sinners.
He rose again, defeating death and opening the way to reconciliation with God for those who trust in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that our sins are insignificant.
But that Christ is sufficient.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that forgiveness is available.
Not that consequences automatically disappear.
But that condemnation does not have the final word for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).
Grace does not teach us how to hide our scandals more effectively.
Grace teaches us how to stop living in them.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
The grace that forgives is also the grace that teaches us to change.
So if you have taken something that was never yours, return it where possible.
If you have deceived someone, tell the truth.
If you have wounded someone, acknowledge the damage.
If you have violated a covenant, repent sincerely and seek appropriate accountability.
If you have been using God's forgiveness as an excuse to continue harming others, remember that biblical repentance is more than feeling sorry when you are caught.
It involves a genuine turning toward God.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia expresses repentance, a change of mind and heart that, in its biblical context, calls us toward a changed direction in life.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot demand that everyone immediately trust you again.
You cannot guarantee that every broken relationship will be restored.
But through Jesus Christ, your past does not have to determine the spiritual direction of your future.
And if you are the person who was wounded by someone else's deception, remember that forgiveness does not require you to abandon wisdom, safety, accountability, or healthy boundaries.
God sees the person who was harmed, too.
Sarah was not forgotten in this story.
God knew her situation even when Abraham's actions placed her in danger.
There are moments when the people who should protect us fail us.
There are moments when the people who speak about God wound us.
But their failure does not define the character of Jesus.
Do not confuse the imperfections of His followers with the perfection of the Savior.
Perhaps this is the message someone on your Facebook timeline desperately needs today.
Someone is hiding behind a respectable reputation.
Someone is carrying the consequences of another person's decisions.
Someone believes their past has disqualified them from ever being loved by God.
Someone is silently wondering whether there is still a way home.
Let your social media become more than a collection of photographs, arguments, entertainment, and temporary distractions.
Let it become a place where someone might encounter biblical truth when they need it most.

Ministry requires more than good intentions. Creating biblical resources, expanding discipleship initiatives, and consistently bringing Scripture-centered encouragement to people requires time, labor, and practical support.

Paul recognized the importance of supporting those who labor in proclaiming the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that Christian giving should come willingly from the heart, not through compulsion.
It is not a payment for salvation.
It is not a purchase of God's favor.
It is not a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church, family, or those in need.
Helping biblical truth reach more people.
Helping believers grow deeper roots.
Helping those wounded by life discover that the Gospel speaks to their brokenness.
Helping someone who thinks they are beyond redemption encounter the message of Jesus Christ.
And if you cannot contribute financially right now, never believe that your prayers, encouragement, or willingness to share the Gospel are insignificant.

The Gospel is for the wealthy and the poor, the respected and the rejected, the strong and the exhausted, the person who has walked with God for decades and the person who is taking their first trembling steps toward Him.
Before you leave, ask yourself one question.
What part of your life are you still trying to protect through fear, deception, or control instead of surrendering it to Jesus?
Abraham had promises, yet he struggled with fear.
Abimelech had authority, yet he needed divine restraint.
An entire household experienced affliction, yet God brought healing.
And through it all, God's faithfulness remained greater than human failure.
That is why your story does not have to end at the chapter you are most ashamed of.
There is still a Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
There is still mercy for those who come to Him.
There is still forgiveness through His blood.
There is still hope beyond the wreckage of human failure.
Come out of hiding.
Bring the truth into the light.
Surrender what you have been desperately trying to control.
Let Jesus confront what needs confronting, forgive what needs forgiving, and transform what needs transforming.
Because the greatest miracle is not merely that God can restore what sin has damaged.
It is that He can transform the very heart that once caused the damage.
Your scandal may explain the tears on yesterday's pages, but it does not have the authority to write the final chapter of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
